title: How we worked out chameleon colour
tagline: From Aristotle’s puff of air to nerves, pigment cells, and the nanocrystals found in 2015.
intro: For two thousand years people believed chameleons copied their surroundings and lived on air. Nineteenth-century physiologists found pigment cells and the nerves that steer them, and twentieth-century field biologists showed the colours are messages. In 2015 physicists and biologists in Geneva showed the brightest colours come from a tunable crystal lattice in the skin.

eras.name: Myths and first looks
eras.summary: Ancient writers describe chameleons, and the air-diet and background-copying myths take hold.

eras.name: Nerves and pigment cells
eras.summary: Naturalists name species, physiologists find colour cells and the nerves that control them, and India protects its wildlife.

eras.name: What the colours mean
eras.summary: Field studies show colour change is mostly for signals and temperature, not for matching backgrounds.

eras.name: Crystals, copies and protection
eras.summary: Nanocrystals explain the colours, engineers copy them, and laws tighten against the pet trade.

events.title: Colour from a puff of air
events.text: In his History of Animals, Aristotle described the chameleon carefully: its eyes, its feet, its body. He wrote that its colour changes when it fills itself with air, turning black, ochre or spotted like a panther, all over the body.
events.why: It was the first careful written account of chameleon colour change.

events.title: “Every colour except red and white”
events.text: Pliny’s Natural History said the chameleon takes the colour of whatever it is touching, except red and white, and repeated the old idea that it lives on air. Later naturalists noted that he copied Aristotle, less accurately.
events.why: The background-matching myth has followed chameleons ever since.

events.title: A doctor doubts the air diet
events.text: In Pseudodoxia Epidemica, a book of common errors, Browne argued that chameleons cannot live on air and must eat like other animals.
events.why: An early push to test old animal stories against evidence.

events.title: India’s chameleon gets its name
events.text: Laurenti described Chamaeleo zeylanicus, the chameleon of India and Sri Lanka (zeylanicus means ‘of Ceylon’).
events.why: It gave India’s only chameleon the scientific name it still carries.

events.title: Live chameleons from Cairo
events.text: The Vienna Academy obtained ten live chameleons from Cairo and gave six to the physiologist Brücke. He presented a study of how African chameleons change colour, comparing them with cephalopods, and described colour cells moving their pigment.
events.why: It turned the chameleon’s colour change into a problem for laboratory physiology.

events.title: Nerves steer the colour
events.text: Bert reported that coloured grains move toward or away from the skin’s surface, steered by two sets of nerves. When he cut the pathway at the base of the brain, the whole chameleon turned black and stopped changing.
events.why: It showed that the brain controls colour change through nerves.

events.title: Cuttlefish colour in a flash
events.who: A. V. Hill and D. Y. Solandt
events.text: Working on cuttlefish, Hill and Solandt showed that their colour cells are pulled open by muscles and change in well under a second (as cited in later reviews).
events.why: It set up the contrast with chameleons, whose colour cells have no muscles.

events.title: India protects its wildlife
events.text: The Wild Life (Protection) Act listed animals in schedules with different levels of protection. The Indian chameleon came to be listed in Schedule II (Part I), making it illegal to catch, keep or trade.
events.why: It made the Indian chameleon a legally protected animal.

events.title: Colour and temperature
events.who: B. Michael Walton and Albert F. Bennett
events.text: Studying chameleons from Kenya, Walton and Bennett found that skin reflectance changes with temperature in some species: paler when hot, darker when cool.
events.why: It showed colour change also helps chameleons manage heat.

events.title: Female colours say yes or no
events.text: Radio-tracking and painting female common chameleons, Cuadrado showed that their temporary colours track their breeding state, and males respond to them.
events.why: It proved female chameleon colours are messages to males.

events.title: How cephalopods paint themselves
events.text: Messenger’s big review explained how octopus and cuttlefish chromatophores work: elastic pigment sacs pulled open by radial muscles wired to the brain, closing again by recoil.
events.why: It became the standard account of the fastest colour change in animals.

events.title: Colour change evolved for talking
events.text: Comparing 21 lineages of South African dwarf chameleons, they found that the species with the biggest colour changes were those with the showiest social signals, not those living on the most varied backgrounds.
events.why: It gave strong evidence against the background-matching myth.

events.title: Brighter, faster males win
events.text: Filming contests between ten male veiled chameleons, they found the side stripes predicted which male would approach, while head brightness and the speed of head colour change predicted the winner.
events.why: It showed different body parts send different messages.

events.title: India’s chameleon: Least Concern
events.who: IUCN Red List assessors (Srinivasulu and colleagues)
events.text: The IUCN Red List assessed the Indian chameleon as Least Concern, while regional studies noted it is rare in places such as Rajasthan and Sri Lanka.
events.why: It recorded the species’ status for conservation planning.

events.title: A third of chameleons threatened
events.text: An assessment of 184 of the roughly 200 known chameleon species found about 36% threatened with extinction. Around 85 species live only in Madagascar.
events.why: It showed how many chameleons depend on shrinking forests.

events.title: The colour is in the crystals
events.who: Jérémie Teyssier, Suzanne Saenko, Dirk van der Marel and Michel Milinkovitch
events.text: Electron microscopes showed guanine nanocrystals about 127 nm across in a triangular lattice inside panther chameleon iridophores. In excited males the crystals sit about 30% further apart, so the reflected colour shifts from blue toward yellow and red. Salty baths reversed it.
events.why: It showed chameleon colour change is mainly structural, not pigment.

events.title: A built-in sunshade
events.text: The same study found a deeper layer of iridophores with bigger, messier crystals that reflects much of the sun’s near-infrared light: about 45% of that energy in panther chameleons.
events.why: It suggested the skin also guards against overheating.

events.title: The fastest tongues are the smallest
events.text: Filming 20 species, Anderson found small chameleons have the most explosive tongues, with peak accelerations up to 264 g, powered by elastic tissue loaded like a spring.
events.why: It showed the tongue is a spring-loaded catapult.

events.title: Every chameleon under CITES
events.text: A proposal to CITES noted that all chameleons except the African pygmy chameleons were already listed in Appendix II (with one Madagascar species in Appendix I), and proposed adding the last ones.
events.why: International trade in chameleons needs permits under the treaty.

events.title: A smart skin copies the trick
events.text: Inspired by chameleon skin, chemists at Emory University made a stretchy material whose colour changes in heat and sunlight while keeping its size.
events.why: Chameleon physics became a design idea for new materials.

events.title: A film of plant crystals
events.who: Researchers publishing in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces
events.text: A flexible film made from cellulose nanocrystals changed colour from blue to red when stretched, pressed or made damp.
events.why: It showed renewable materials can do the trick too.

events.title: The nano-chameleon
events.text: Brookesia nana was described from Madagascar. The male measures 13.5 mm from snout to vent, about 22 mm with its tail, one of the smallest reptiles known.
events.why: It shows how varied Madagascar’s chameleons are.

events.title: Schedule I for India’s chameleon
events.text: The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 redrew the schedules. The Indian chameleon is now listed in Schedule I, the highest level of protection.
events.why: It strengthened protection against catching and trading the species.

events.title: Chameleons in a suitcase
events.text: Customs officers at Chennai airport found 22 snakes and a chameleon in a passenger’s checked bags from Kuala Lumpur. The animals were seized under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
events.why: It shows the illegal reptile trade passes through India’s airports.

facts: The crystals that colour a chameleon are about 127 nanometres across, hundreds of times thinner than a hair.
In excited male panther chameleons, the gaps between the crystals grow by about 30%.
A deep layer of the skin reflects about 45% of the sun’s near-infrared energy in panther chameleons.
Chameleons do not change colour to match their background: the big changes are signals and temperature control.
India has just one chameleon species, Chamaeleo zeylanicus.
The male nano-chameleon Brookesia nana is 13.5 mm from snout to vent.
Small chameleons shoot their tongues with peak accelerations up to 264 g.
The red-headed garden lizard that many call a chameleon is not one: it is an agamid.
